site.title: Mythcraft
site.description: Practical guides on Mythcraft, organized for fast browsing and comparison.

pages.title: Myths and misconcept
pages.summary: Myths and misconceptions are not just “wrong facts”. They are durable stories, shortcuts or explanations that feel true enough to survive correction.

pages.title: Influencers
pages.summary: People often use a familiar person's confidence as a shortcut for credibility, especially online.

pages.title: Local Voices
pages.summary: Corrections work better when accurate information comes from people the audience already recognizes and trusts.

pages.title: Check First
pages.summary: Many creators share information without systematic verification, even when their audience treats the post like researched advice.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Influencers.

pages.title: Lane Drift
pages.summary: Audiences can mistake trust in a creator's lifestyle, politics, or fitness content for expertise on unrelated evidence-heavy claims.

pages.title: Felt Trust
pages.summary: A familiar creator can make health advice feel personal and caring even when the claim needs medical expertise.

pages.title: Viral Proof
pages.summary: High engagement can make a weak claim feel safer to trust before viewers have checked what the post actually proves.

pages.title: Backfire
pages.summary: Clear corrections usually reduce false belief, even though badly designed debunking can still fail.

pages.title: Correction Decay
pages.summary: A correction can be accurate at first but lose ground when the false story keeps returning through media, peers or elites.

pages.title: Distrust Risk
pages.summary: Corrections are most fragile when the audience sees the source as hostile, manipulative or poorly justified.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Backfire.

pages.title: Study Evidence
pages.summary: Large experiments and reviews suggest factual corrections usually improve accuracy and that true backfire is rare.

pages.title: Naming Myths
pages.summary: Good debunking names the false claim clearly enough to correct it but keeps the true claim as the message people remember.

pages.title: Political Corrections
pages.summary: Political corrections can improve factual accuracy while still leaving identity, trust and voting attitudes largely unchanged.

pages.title: Commercial Myths
pages.summary: Myths gain authority when they are packaged as training, products or practical solutions for busy professionals.

pages.title: Brain based
pages.summary: Words such as brain-based and neural can make a weak education claim sound scientific before it has been fairly tested.

pages.title: Brain Gym
pages.summary: Movement breaks may be sensible, but branded brain-integration claims need evidence that ordinary activity does not provide.

pages.title: “Evidence Based”
pages.summary: A product is not proven just because it cites research on a broad principle such as feedback, motivation or practice.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Commercial Myths.

pages.title: Learning styles
pages.summary: Learning-style labels can feel useful, but the evidence does not support matching lessons to fixed sensory types.

pages.title: Adoption paths
pages.summary: Training days, consultancy networks and ready-made materials can help weak claims spread because they are easy to buy and use.

pages.title: Common Sense
pages.summary: A claim can feel sensible because it simplifies experience, not because reliable sources support it.

pages.title: Accuracy prompts
pages.summary: Small accuracy reminders can improve what people share by shifting attention from plausibility and identity toward verification.

pages.title: Full moons
pages.summary: Full-moon beliefs show how vivid memories can overpower fair comparison when ordinary nights are not counted.

pages.title: Hindsight
pages.summary: Hindsight bias lets people build convincing explanations after an outcome, even when the same logic could predict the opposite.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Common Sense.

pages.title: Learning styles
pages.summary: Learning preferences may feel personal, but the key claim fails when matched teaching does not reliably improve outcomes.

pages.title: Prediction test
pages.summary: A claim becomes stronger when it says what should happen, what should not happen, and what evidence would count against it.

pages.title: Concept Change
pages.summary: Students often need help replacing a mistaken model, not just adding correct facts on top of it.

pages.title: Conflict
pages.summary: Surprising evidence helps only when students compare predictions, evidence, and a stronger replacement explanation.

pages.title: Diagnostics
pages.summary: Good diagnostic questions expose the model behind an answer, not just whether a student chose the right option.

pages.title: Everyday Models
pages.summary: Students often keep wrong science ideas because the models still make everyday experiences feel explainable.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Concept Change.

pages.title: Private Universe
pages.summary: The seasons-and-moon-phase interviews show how confident learners can retain private explanations after years of instruction.

pages.title: Replacement
pages.summary: Students need a better model they can use across examples, diagrams, predictions, and unfamiliar cases.

pages.title: Tone
pages.summary: Even accurate corrections can fail when they make people feel attacked, embarrassed or talked down to.

pages.title: Face saving
pages.summary: Face-saving corrections make it easier to accept better information without treating the original mistake as a personal failure.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Tone.

pages.title: Intent
pages.summary: Treating every false claim as deliberate deception can make honest mistakes harder to repair and bad actors harder to identify.

pages.title: Public replies
pages.summary: Public correction can inform bystanders, but ridicule and quote-post dunking can turn fact-checking into a status fight.

pages.title: Reactance
pages.summary: A correction framed as contempt or pressure can make people defend their autonomy instead of reconsidering the claim.

pages.title: Replacements
pages.summary: The strongest corrections do more than say a myth is wrong; they give readers a clearer explanation to use instead.

pages.title: Old Stories
pages.summary: A myth can keep shaping judgement after correction when the debunking removes a story without replacing it.

pages.title: Memory Gap
pages.summary: People may recall that a claim was false while still using it to judge motives, risks or blame.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Old Stories.

pages.title: Myth vs Fact
pages.summary: Myth-versus-fact formats can fail when the false claim remains more vivid and complete than the correction.

pages.title: Replacement
pages.summary: Corrections work better when they give readers a simple alternative account to use instead of the myth.

pages.title: Old Causes
pages.summary: A false cause can keep guiding people's explanations even after they remember that it was corrected.

pages.title: Fire Study
pages.summary: The classic warehouse fire experiment shows how a corrected detail can still explain explosions, fumes and severity.

pages.title: Timing
pages.summary: Fast, clear correction can limit damage, but rushed debunking can also confuse people if evidence is still uncertain.

pages.title: Amplification
pages.summary: Some rumours need public correction, while others are better handled quietly before a wider audience sees them.

pages.title: High harm
pages.summary: Health, safety, finance and voting rumours can require faster action because people may act before a full debunk is ready.

pages.title: Holding fixes
pages.summary: A holding correction can reduce harm early by separating what is known, unknown and safest to do next.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Timing.

pages.title: Late labels
pages.summary: Labels and context boxes can help, but they arrive too late if a false post has already done most of its travelling.

pages.title: Familiarity
pages.summary: Familiarity can make a myth feel credible even when people no longer remember where it came from.

pages.title: Teacher Corrections
pages.summary: Specific, evidence-based interventions can reduce belief in education myths when they explain the problem clearly.

pages.title: Practice gap
pages.summary: Teachers may reject a myth on a survey while old labels, worksheets and school routines keep the practice alive.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Teacher Corrections.

pages.title: Learning styles
pages.summary: The strongest corrections separate real pupil preferences from the unsupported claim that matching sensory styles improves learning.

pages.title: Personalised fixes
pages.summary: Personalised myth correction may support conceptual change, but repeated exposure to weakly held myths can increase familiarity.

pages.title: Refutation texts
pages.summary: Refutation texts work best when they name the myth, reject it clearly and replace it with a better explanation teachers can use.

pages.title: Training design
pages.summary: Durable correction needs pre-checks, clear refutation, replacement practices, follow-up coaching and audits of old materials.

pages.title: Expert Trust
pages.summary: Health beliefs can become durable when a trusted professional, institution or expert-sounding source appears to support them.

pages.title: AI Doctors
pages.summary: AI-made doctor videos can attach fake medical authority to supplements, cures, and health claims at social media speed.

pages.title: False Balance
pages.summary: A myth can look stronger than it is when one dissenting expert is presented as equal to a field's wider judgement.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Expert Trust.

pages.title: One Doctor
pages.summary: A single credentialed voice can make a weak health claim feel credible long after journals, regulators, or evidence have moved on.

pages.title: Surgisphere
pages.summary: The Surgisphere retractions show how respected journals can briefly amplify unreliable health claims before scrutiny catches up.

pages.title: MMR Case
pages.summary: The MMR-autism myth shows how a prestigious journal, a doctor, and media attention can give a false claim lasting public power.

pages.title: Fact Checks
pages.summary: Fact-checking matters, but false claims are cheap to produce and costly to correct at scale.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Fact Checks.

pages.title: Speed Gap
pages.summary: False claims can be produced and reshared faster than careful fact-checks can investigate, explain, and reach the same audience.

pages.title: Mutation
pages.summary: A corrected myth can survive by changing examples, wording, screenshots, or messengers while keeping the same underlying story.

pages.title: Platforms
pages.summary: Ranking, recommendation, monetisation, and moderation choices can either amplify myths or make reliable context easier to find.

pages.title: Prebunking
pages.summary: Prebunking prepares people to recognise manipulation tactics before a false claim reaches them, reducing dependence on later corrections.

pages.title: Better Story
pages.summary: Corrections are stronger when they do more than say what is false; they explain what really happened and why the myth seemed plausible.

pages.title: Debunking
pages.summary: Good corrections state the truth, warn about the false claim and explain what actually accounts for the confusion.

pages.title: Fact first
pages.summary: A correction headline works best when it gives the true answer before briefly naming the false claim it replaces.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Debunking.

pages.title: The trick
pages.summary: A strong correction shows the trick behind a claim, such as cherry-picking, false context, edited media, or source confusion.

pages.title: Health myths
pages.summary: Public health teams use truth-sandwich corrections to answer rumours without making the misinformation the main message.

pages.title: Replacement
pages.summary: People are more likely to drop a misconception when the correction gives them a clearer story to remember instead.

pages.title: Name it
pages.summary: A debunk should identify a myth only when readers need that label to understand the correction.

pages.title: Falling Objects
pages.summary: Some false beliefs last because everyday experience seems to confirm them until the hidden conditions are made clear.

pages.title: Moon Drop
pages.summary: The Moon demonstration made the missing condition visible by removing almost all air resistance from the fall.

pages.title: Paper Shape
pages.summary: A flat sheet and a crumpled sheet reveal why shape can matter more than mass in everyday falling.

pages.title: Home Tests
pages.summary: Simple drop tests can show when mass matters less than air resistance, as long as the examples are chosen carefully.

pages.title: Galileo
pages.summary: Galileo's real achievement was controlled measurement, not just a dramatic tower-drop legend.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Falling Objects.

pages.title: Terminal Speed
pages.summary: Terminal velocity explains why some objects stop accelerating in air even though gravity keeps pulling them downward.

pages.title: False Balance
pages.summary: Giving weak claims equal weight with strong evidence can make a misconception look like a live debate.

pages.title: Climate Debate
pages.summary: Climate reporting became a prominent example of how balanced formats can exaggerate scientific disagreement.

pages.title: Due Impartiality
pages.summary: Editorial standards distinguish between representing relevant viewpoints and giving every viewpoint equal weight.

pages.title: Equal Airtime
pages.summary: Giving opposing voices the same visibility can make weak claims appear as credible as a much stronger evidence base.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on False Balance.

pages.title: Vaccine Coverage
pages.summary: Experiments found that balanced vaccine coverage could make readers think experts were more divided than they were.

pages.title: Evidence Weighting
pages.summary: Weight-of-evidence approaches help audiences see where the strongest support lies without hiding disagreement.

pages.title: Health Claims
pages.summary: Health misinformation often spreads because people believe they are helping friends or family avoid harm.

pages.title: Cancer Stories
pages.summary: Personal cancer recovery stories can offer hope while hiding treatment details that make a cure claim unsafe.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Health Claims.

pages.title: Kind Corrections
pages.summary: Correcting a health myth from someone close works better when the response protects the relationship as well as the facts.

pages.title: Natural Remedies
pages.summary: Natural remedy claims can sound gentle and harmless, even when they create false confidence or delay useful care.

pages.title: Urgent Warnings
pages.summary: Urgent health warnings can feel like protection, but speed often beats verification when fear and care are mixed together.

pages.title: Vaccine Fears
pages.summary: Vaccine myths can become persuasive when refusal is framed as a loving parent's safest choice.

pages.title: Familiarity
pages.summary: Repeated claims can feel true because familiarity makes them easier to process, even when the evidence is weak.

pages.title: After Correction
pages.summary: A false claim can keep its familiar ring after correction unless the accurate replacement becomes easier to remember.

pages.title: Headlines
pages.summary: Even a single prior encounter with a headline can make it feel more accurate later, especially when people read in passing.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Familiarity.

pages.title: Fluency
pages.summary: Processing fluency explains why claims that feel easy to read, recall, or recognise can be mistaken for claims that are true.

pages.title: Climate Claims
pages.summary: Climate misinformation shows how repetition can raise truth ratings for familiar claims without changing someone's whole worldview.

pages.title: Better Corrections
pages.summary: Good corrections lead with the truth, identify the trap carefully, and give readers a clearer explanation to remember.

pages.title: Identity
pages.summary: People often judge claims through trust, community and identity as much as through evidence alone.

pages.title: Expert Limits
pages.summary: A credible professional can accidentally lend authority to a false claim when they speak confidently beyond what they actually know.

pages.title: Family Advice
pages.summary: Health myths can feel safest when they come from parents or relatives who shaped a person's earliest ideas about care and risk.

pages.title: Group Loyalty
pages.summary: Some myths persist because accepting or rejecting them signals loyalty, courage, compassion, scepticism, or belonging.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Identity.

pages.title: Influencers
pages.summary: Online creators can feel personally trustworthy even when their fact-checking routines are weak or invisible to followers.

pages.title: Trusted Fixes
pages.summary: Corrections work better when they protect the listener's dignity while separating a trusted person from a false claim.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Myths and misconcept 0 d48 d7.

pages.title: Learning Styles
pages.summary: Students may have preferences, but matching teaching to fixed learning styles is not supported as a reliable learning strategy.

pages.title: Content first
pages.summary: Diagrams, discussion, sound, movement and practice can all help, but the best choice usually depends on the subject matter and learning goal.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Learning Styles.

pages.title: Labels risk
pages.summary: A label meant to support a child can quietly shape what adults expect them to enjoy, attempt or succeed at in school.

pages.title: Matching claim
pages.summary: The key claim is not that students differ, but that matching instruction to a style improves learning, and that claim has not held up.

pages.title: Self labels
pages.summary: Students may avoid useful study strategies when a style label becomes part of how they explain success and difficulty.

pages.title: Survey trap
pages.summary: Style inventories can make personalisation look precise while pulling attention away from explanations, practice and feedback.

pages.title: Teacher Belief
pages.summary: High reported belief in learning styles shows how an unsupported idea can become normal in professional culture.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Teacher Belief.

pages.title: Learner labels
pages.summary: Calling a pupil a visual or auditory learner can turn a weak theory into a fixed label that narrows effort and strategy.

pages.title: Survey wording
pages.summary: Small changes in survey wording can blur preferences, variety and the stronger matching claim that evidence reviews reject.

pages.title: Teacher belief
pages.summary: Belief in learning styles appears high among both qualified teachers and people still entering the profession.

pages.title: Correction
pages.summary: Correction can reduce endorsement sharply when it explains the matching claim and gives teachers usable alternatives.

pages.title: Reported use
pages.summary: The Wellcome survey shows how learning styles moved from belief into lesson planning and classroom routines.

pages.title: Left Brain
pages.summary: Left-brain and right-brain learner labels oversimplify brain function and can distract from better teaching choices.

pages.title: Imaging study
pages.summary: A large imaging study found local left and right brain patterns, not a global split between left-brained and right-brained people.

pages.title: Learner labels
pages.summary: Calling a child left-brained or right-brained can turn a temporary preference into a false limit on what they are expected to learn.

pages.title: Lateralisation
pages.summary: Brain functions can be partly lateralised, but that does not mean people learn through one dominant hemisphere.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Left Brain.

pages.title: Style matching
pages.summary: Teaching works best when methods fit the material and task, not when they are matched to a claimed brain style.

pages.title: Creativity myth
pages.summary: Creativity depends on integrated thinking across both hemispheres, not a special right-brain mode teachers can switch on.

pages.title: Media Literacy
pages.summary: Media literacy helps people ask better questions before a false claim becomes familiar and emotionally anchored.

pages.title: Emotional Headlines
pages.summary: Strong emotion is not proof of falsehood, but outrage, fear, and simple villains are signals to slow down before believing or sharing.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Media Literacy.

pages.title: Lateral reading
pages.summary: Lateral reading helps readers check who is behind a claim before polished design or confident wording makes it feel credible.

pages.title: Practice limits
pages.summary: Media literacy can be taught, but one-off lessons are weaker than repeated practice across changing platforms and formats.

pages.title: Prebunking
pages.summary: Prebunking teaches people to recognize familiar misinformation tactics before a specific false claim becomes memorable.

pages.title: SIFT method
pages.summary: The SIFT method turns media literacy into a simple routine: stop, investigate, find better coverage, and trace the claim.

pages.title: Memory
pages.summary: Memory is reconstructive, so confident recall is not the same as a perfect recording of events.

pages.title: Confidence
pages.summary: Confidence can matter most when recorded early under fair conditions, but later confidence may reflect contamination.

pages.title: Fair Lineups
pages.summary: Lineup design can reduce suggestion by limiting cues that point witnesses toward a suspect before memory is tested.

pages.title: Flashbulb Memory
pages.summary: Vivid memories of shocking events can feel photographic while still changing in important details over time.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Memory.

pages.title: Leading Questions
pages.summary: Small wording changes after an event can steer what witnesses later remember without making them dishonest.

pages.title: Retelling
pages.summary: Retelling a story can make it feel clearer and more convincing even when the remembered details have shifted.

pages.title: Mental Models
pages.summary: Misconceptions can feel stable because they fit into a wider model of how the world works.

pages.title: Better Story
pages.summary: Effective debunking gives people a clearer alternative explanation instead of leaving the old myth as the only complete story.

pages.title: Earth Models
pages.summary: Children's Earth models show how wrong ideas can be creative attempts to reconcile teaching with everyday experience.

pages.title: Contradictions
pages.summary: Some conspiracy models survive correction by treating official denials, failed predictions, and expert consensus as part of the plot.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Mental Models.

pages.title: Natural Myths
pages.summary: Natural health myths feel convincing when safety, distrust, and personal testimony all reinforce the same simple model.

pages.title: Retracted Causes
pages.summary: A retracted detail can keep guiding judgment when it still fills the missing cause in a person's story of what happened.

pages.title: False Info
pages.summary: The difference between accidental falsehood and deliberate deception matters because each needs a different response.

pages.title: Overcalling
pages.summary: Calling a false claim disinformation requires evidence of deliberate deception, not just proof that the claim is wrong.

pages.title: Flood tactics
pages.summary: Organised deception can work by confusing and exhausting people, not just by making them believe one false claim.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on False Info.

pages.title: Intent test
pages.summary: The same false claim can need a correction, an investigation, or both, depending on whether error or deception is driving it.

pages.title: Platform risk
pages.summary: Modern platform rules increasingly target networks, incentives, algorithms, and transparency gaps rather than single false posts alone.

pages.title: Better fixes
pages.summary: Corrections are more persuasive when they explain what really happened instead of only saying a claim is false.

pages.title: Analogies
pages.summary: Analogies can make difficult ideas easier, but they can also leave learners with the wrong model.

pages.title: Analogy Overextension
pages.summary: Learners may falsely generalize features of one system to another, building shallow understanding anchored on familiar comparisons.

pages.title: Geologic Time
pages.summary: Compressing billions of years into a spatial diagram can lead learners to misjudge the timing of evolutionary events.

pages.title: Historical Metaphors
pages.summary: Persistent analogies in historical scientific discourse shaped methods and interpretations, sometimes embedding misconceptions into the field.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Analogies.

pages.title: Plumbing Analogy
pages.summary: Using pipes as an analogy for blood flow can mislead learners about vessel flexibility and pressure dynamics.

pages.title: Teaching Analogy Limits
pages.summary: Explicitly showing which features of an analogy map and which do not helps learners avoid misconceptions.

pages.title: Key Terms
pages.summary: Myths are widely repeated false stories, while misconceptions are mistaken understandings that may be sincere.

pages.title: Better Corrections
pages.summary: Myths often need public reframing, while misconceptions usually need a better explanation that fills the gap left behind.

pages.title: Cultural Myths
pages.summary: Some false claims survive because they become familiar stories that people repeat before they ever check the evidence.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Key Terms.

pages.title: Mistaken Models
pages.summary: A misconception often persists because it gives people a simple working explanation that fits what they think they see.

pages.title: Tell Them Apart
pages.summary: A practical test asks whether a belief mainly spreads through repetition or mainly rests on a mistaken explanation.

pages.title: Myth to Model
pages.summary: A repeated claim can become the starting point for a larger mistaken model about health, intelligence, history or science.

pages.title: Neuromyths
pages.summary: Brain-based claims can look scientific while oversimplifying what neuroscience actually says about learning.

pages.title: Brain Gym
pages.summary: Movement breaks can help classrooms, but Brain Gym-style claims about hemispheric integration go beyond the evidence.

pages.title: Critical periods
pages.summary: Critical period myths can make learning difficulties seem time-limited when development is usually more flexible and gradual.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Neuromyths.

pages.title: Learning styles
pages.summary: Learning styles feel respectful of pupil differences, but matching lessons to fixed sensory types has not shown reliable learning gains.

pages.title: Brain labels
pages.summary: Left-brain and right-brain labels turn real hemispheric differences into misleading learner types that can narrow expectations.

pages.title: Training rubrics
pages.summary: Neuromyths spread when training templates and observation rubrics treat weak brain claims as professional standards.

pages.title: Campaigns
pages.summary: Deliberate deception may require platform, policy and institutional responses as well as individual fact-checking.

pages.title: Astroturfing
pages.summary: Astroturfing makes organised persuasion look like ordinary public support, changing how rumours, protests and policy debates are judged.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Campaigns.

pages.title: IRA Case
pages.summary: The Russian Internet Research Agency showed how fake identities, targeted pages and existing social divisions can turn deception into mass influence.

pages.title: Platform Rules
pages.summary: Behaviour-based rules can reduce fake accounts, hidden ads and artificial amplification while leaving room for lawful disagreement.

pages.title: Prebunking
pages.summary: Prebunking prepares people to recognise emotional manipulation, scapegoating and false choices before a campaign reaches them.

pages.title: Media Coverage
pages.summary: Careful reporting can explain a rumour's origin, uncertainty and amplification pattern without making the false claim more memorable.

pages.title: Anecdotes
pages.summary: Many misconceptions begin when a real experience is stretched into a rule that evidence does not support.

pages.title: Safety reports
pages.summary: Safety reports can reveal warning signals, but raw reports cannot prove that a vaccine or drug caused an event.

pages.title: Health stories
pages.summary: Health stories can feel more convincing than stronger evidence because fear, pain and hope make single cases easier to trust.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Anecdotes.

pages.title: Small samples
pages.summary: A few memorable examples can look like a rule when small samples are expected to represent the wider world too neatly.

pages.title: Timing trap
pages.summary: A real improvement after a remedy can still be coincidence unless the cause is tested against what would have happened anyway.

pages.title: Story limits
pages.summary: Anecdotes are useful as signals, examples and questions, but they become misleading when used to settle general claims.

pages.title: Platform Design
pages.summary: Design decisions around friction, labels, recommendations and sharing can change how far myths travel.

pages.title: Accuracy Nudges
pages.summary: Accuracy prompts work by reminding users to consider truth, not just emotion, identity or social approval, before passing news along.

pages.title: Community Notes
pages.summary: Community notes can add trusted context to misleading posts, but fast-moving myths may outrun the rating process that makes notes visible.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Platform Design.

pages.title: Sharing Prompts
pages.summary: A small pause before reposting can reduce myth spread by shifting users from impulse to attention at the moment a claim travels.

pages.title: Algorithms
pages.summary: Recommendation systems can amplify myths when they optimize for engagement, or limit them when ranking signals value reliability and harm reduction.

pages.title: Warning Labels
pages.summary: Warning labels can lower belief in false claims, but vague or distrusted labels may fail or even harden group resistance.

pages.title: Politics
pages.summary: Political myths are hard to correct when accepting the correction feels like rejecting a group or worldview.

pages.title: Smart Defenses
pages.summary: More knowledge can sometimes make people better at protecting identity-aligned conclusions rather than abandoning them.

pages.title: After Fact Checks
pages.summary: A correction may weaken one false claim while leaving the larger distrustful story that made it persuasive intact.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Politics.

pages.title: Low Conflict
pages.summary: Corrections work better when they let people reconsider a claim without feeling humiliated, attacked, or expelled from their group.

pages.title: Group Cues
pages.summary: Likes, shares, replies, and silence can make a false claim feel socially approved before anyone checks the evidence.

pages.title: Social Risk
pages.summary: Accepting a correction can threaten friendships, family ties, status, and belonging when a myth has become a group signal.

pages.title: Prebunking
pages.summary: Prebunking teaches people the tricks behind misleading claims before they encounter a specific myth.

pages.title: Bad News game
pages.summary: Playing the role of a misinformation producer can make manipulation tactics more visible when readers encounter them later.

pages.title: Election rumours
pages.summary: Election prebunks work best when they point voters toward official dates, locations, and vote-counting channels before rumours spread.

pages.title: Emotion cues
pages.summary: Emotional prebunks teach readers to spot outrage, fear, or disgust cues before those feelings turn into belief or sharing.

pages.title: Fact vs tactic
pages.summary: Some warnings target a likely false claim, while others teach a reusable trick that can travel across topics.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Prebunking.

pages.title: Fading effects
pages.summary: A prebunk can improve recognition of manipulation, but its effects may weaken unless people see reminders in the right places.

pages.title: Rumour Gaps
pages.summary: Corrections work better when they fill the explanatory gap that made the rumour useful in the first place.

pages.title: Bare Denials
pages.summary: A correction can reduce belief yet still leave people using the old rumour when it remains the only available explanation.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Rumour Gaps.

pages.title: Outbreak Origins
pages.summary: Outbreak rumours are easier to correct when evidence about genetics and transmission gives people a plausible origin story.

pages.title: Uncertainty
pages.summary: Saying what is known, unknown, and still being tested can replace false certainty without pretending the evidence is complete.

pages.title: Vote Delays
pages.summary: Explaining ballot verification and counting steps can replace a fraud rumour with a clearer account of why delays happen.

pages.title: Fire Scenario
pages.summary: The warehouse fire scenario shows how people can remember a correction but still rely on a disproved cause when explaining events.

pages.title: Study Practice
pages.summary: Evidence-backed study practices offer a stronger route to learning than sorting students into fixed styles.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Study Practice.

pages.title: Style surveys
pages.summary: Students may prefer certain formats, but preference alone does not show that matching instruction improves achievement.

pages.title: Self testing
pages.summary: Rereading can feel fluent in the moment, but self-testing usually produces stronger delayed recall.

pages.title: Check gaps
pages.summary: Recall activities help teachers spot forgotten knowledge and misconceptions before they become harder to fix.

pages.title: Fit the task
pages.summary: Good teaching often varies format because the task demands it, not because each student has a fixed sensory type.

pages.title: Sciencey Words
pages.summary: Technical words can give myths a false aura of authority when readers cannot easily judge the underlying evidence.

pages.title: Clinically Proven
pages.summary: A label can say 'clinically proven' while hiding whether the tested outcome, comparison group and study quality support the promise.

pages.title: Detox Claims
pages.summary: Detox language often turns real body processes into broad product promises that are hard to measure or falsify.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Sciencey Words.

pages.title: Brain Jargon
pages.summary: Irrelevant brain language can make ordinary explanations feel more satisfying even when it adds no real support.

pages.title: Quantum Claims
pages.summary: Words like 'quantum', 'frequency' and 'resonance' can make vague wellness products sound precise without adding a testable claim.

pages.title: Untestable Claims
pages.summary: A claim that can explain away every failure is protected from evidence rather than supported by it.

pages.title: Slogans
pages.summary: Myths often win because short slogans travel better than the slower, more qualified truth.

pages.title: Emotion
pages.summary: Claims that trigger surprise, anger, pride, or belonging can travel farther because they give people a reason to share.

pages.title: Health Slogans
pages.summary: Simple health rules can mislead when they erase dose, context, trade-offs, and the difference between mild and serious risks.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Slogans.

pages.title: Backfire Risk
pages.summary: Putting the myth first can accidentally advertise it unless the correction leads with the fact and explains the misleading move.

pages.title: Repetition
pages.summary: Repetition can make a false claim feel familiar and believable, even when people have seen corrections before.

pages.title: Corrections
pages.summary: A useful correction does more than say false; it gives people a better explanation they can remember and reuse.

pages.title: Algorithms
pages.summary: Digital platforms can reward emotional, repeatable claims before careful correction has time to catch up.

pages.title: Feed Fixes
pages.summary: Switching away from algorithmic feeds can change what users see, but it may not automatically reduce false belief or polarisation.

pages.title: Metric Gap
pages.summary: Clicks, likes and watch time can reward content people later judge to be unhealthy, misleading or simply not worth seeing.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Algorithms.

pages.title: Creator Rewards
pages.summary: When attention can become followers, revenue or influence, creators have incentives to package myths in repeatable, engaging forms.

pages.title: Outrage Boost
pages.summary: Angry replies can make a false post look important to a ranking system even when many users are trying to reject it.

pages.title: Rumour Loops
pages.summary: A rumour that performs well early can be pushed to wider audiences before verification has time to catch up.

pages.title: 10 Brain
pages.summary: The 10 percent brain claim survives because it turns complex neuroscience into an appealing promise of untapped ability.

pages.title: Brain Damage
pages.summary: Injury and disease show that even small brain areas can matter for language, movement, memory, emotion, and perception.

pages.title: Brain Scans
pages.summary: Brain scans highlight relative changes in activity, not vast silent regions waiting to be switched on.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on 10 Brain.

pages.title: Neuroplasticity
pages.summary: Neuroplasticity means active brain networks can change with experience, not that unused regions contain superhuman abilities.

pages.title: Belief Appeal
pages.summary: The myth works because it turns ordinary learning and effort into a tempting story about hidden reserves waiting to be unlocked.

pages.title: William James
pages.summary: William James wrote about unrealised human potential, but later retellings turned that idea into a false numerical claim about brain use.

pages.title: Uncertainty
pages.summary: Myths often spread during uncertainty because they offer certainty, blame or a rule of thumb when people feel unsettled.

pages.title: Anxiety Effects
pages.summary: Anxiety increases the appeal of explanations that replace ambiguity with a clear story and outcome.

pages.title: Blame Seeking
pages.summary: Assigning responsibility can reduce discomfort when complex events seem confusing or uncontrollable.

pages.title: Fake News
pages.summary: Strong emotional reactions can make false information seem credible even when evidence is available.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Uncertainty.

pages.title: Need Closure
pages.summary: The desire for quick and definite answers can make conspiracy explanations feel emotionally satisfying.

pages.title: Communicating
pages.summary: Clear explanations of what is known and unknown can maintain trust without relying on oversimplified stories.

pages.title: Vaccines
pages.summary: The MMR-autism claim shows why corrections need to explain discredited origins, later evidence and timing confusion.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Vaccines.

pages.title: Large studies
pages.summary: Later studies moved the question from 12 selected children to hundreds of thousands of children without finding increased autism risk.

pages.title: Timing trap
pages.summary: MMR vaccination and visible autism signs can happen in the same early years, making a real sequence feel like proof of cause.

pages.title: Respectful correction
pages.summary: A better correction rejects false vaccine claims while respecting parents and avoiding language that treats autism as a catastrophe.

pages.title: Shifting claims
pages.summary: Claims often move from MMR to thimerosal, mercury or aluminium, but broader reviews still do not support a vaccine-autism link.

pages.title: Wakefield paper
pages.summary: The Wakefield paper became powerful before its weak design, misconduct findings and retraction caught up with its public impact.
